lead: The Laplace transform turns a time signal x(t) into a function X(s) of a complex frequency s = σ + jω. Before integrating, it multiplies x(t) by a decaying factor e<sup>−σt</sup>, so signals that grow too fast for the Fourier transform, such as e<sup>2t</sup>u(t), still have a transform. The integral converges only for some values of s. That set is the region of convergence (ROC), and it is half of the answer: the same X(s) with a different ROC belongs to a different time signal. Circuit, control and filter engineers use the transform because it turns differential equations into algebra.
prereq: You need: the unit step u(t), the impulse δ(t) and real exponentials from the standard signals, and the Fourier transform integral X(jω) = ∫x(t)e<sup>−jωt</sup>dt.

blocks.text: The bilateral (two-sided) Laplace transform of a signal x(t) integrates over all time:
X(s) = ∫ x(t)·e⁻ˢᵗ dt,  t from −∞ to ∞
blocks.where: x(t) is the time signal; s = σ + jω is the complex frequency; σ = Re(s) is the damping in s⁻¹; ω = Im(s) is the angular frequency in rad/s; X(s) is the transform. We write x(t) ↔ X(s) for a transform pair.

blocks.text: Split the kernel: e<sup>−st</sup> = e<sup>−σt</sup>·e<sup>−jωt</sup>. The factor e<sup>−jωt</sup> is the Fourier kernel. The factor e<sup>−σt</sup> damps the signal for t > 0 when σ > 0. So the Laplace transform of x(t) is the Fourier transform of x(t)e<sup>−σt</sup>. Put σ = 0 and you get the Fourier transform: X(jω) = X(s) at s = jω, but only when the ROC contains the jω axis.

The unilateral (one-sided) transform starts at t = 0⁻, just before zero: X(s) = ∫0⁻∞ x(t)e−stdt. For a causal signal (x(t) = 0 for t < 0) the two forms give the same X(s). The one-sided form is the one used to solve differential equations with initial conditions in the properties and LTI-analysis chapters. In this chapter, signals that live at t < 0 always use the bilateral form.

sections.h3: Convergence and the region of convergence

blocks.text: Take the right-sided exponential x(t) = e<sup>−at</sup>u(t), with a real. Only t ≥ 0 contributes:
X(s) = ∫ e⁻⁽ˢ⁺ᵃ⁾ᵗ dt (t from 0 to ∞) = 1/(s + a)
blocks.where: The upper limit gives zero only if e<sup>−(s+a)t</sup> → 0 as t → ∞, that is Re(s + a) > 0. So the ROC is Re(s) > −a, a half-plane to the right of the pole at s = −a.

blocks.text: Now the left-sided signal x(t) = −e<sup>−at</sup>u(−t), which is nonzero only for t < 0. Its integral is −∫<sub>−∞</sub><sup>0</sup> e<sup>−(s+a)t</sup>dt. The antiderivative is e<sup>−(s+a)t</sup>/(s + a), and at t → −∞ the term e<sup>−(s+a)t</sup> vanishes only if Re(s + a) < 0. The result is again 1/(s + a), but with ROC Re(s) < −a, the half-plane to the left of the pole.
So one algebraic expression, 1/(s + a), belongs to two different signals. The ROC tells them apart. This is why an examiner gives no marks for X(s) without its ROC.

sections.h3: Properties of the ROC and standard pairs

blocks.text: Convergence depends only on σ = Re(s), because |e<sup>−st</sup>| = e<sup>−σt</sup>. That one fact gives the rules below. Some syllabi list them as the properties of the ROC.

items: The ROC is a vertical strip σ₁ < Re(s) < σ₂ in the s-plane; σ₁ may be −∞ and σ₂ may be +∞.
The ROC never contains a pole: at a pole X(s) is infinite, so the integral cannot converge there.
A finite-duration signal that is absolutely integrable has the whole s-plane as its ROC.
A right-sided signal has ROC Re(s) > σ₁, to the right of its rightmost pole.
A left-sided signal has ROC Re(s) < σ₂, to the left of its leftmost pole.
A two-sided signal has a strip between two poles, or no ROC at all if the strip is empty.

blocks.text: Figure 4.1.1 draws the three cases for a = 2: the right half-plane, the left half-plane and, for the two-sided signal of the worked example, the strip between −2 and 3.

examples.question: Find the Laplace transform and the ROC of the two-sided signal x(t) = e<sup>−2t</sup>u(t) + e<sup>3t</sup>u(−t). Does its Fourier transform exist? Check X(0) against the area under x(t).
steps: Use the bilateral transform, because the second term lives at t < 0.

Second term: ∫<sub>−∞</sub><sup>0</sup> e<sup>3t</sup>e<sup>−st</sup>dt = ∫<sub>−∞</sub><sup>0</sup> e<sup>(3−s)t</sup>dt = 1/(3 − s), which needs Re(3 − s) > 0, that is Re(s) < 3. Note 1/(3 − s) = −1/(s − 3).
ROC: both terms must converge, so −2 < Re(s) < 3. The strip is not empty, so the transform exists.
Fourier transform: the strip contains σ = 0, so X(jω) = −5/((jω + 2)(jω − 3)) exists.

Check: X(0) = −5/((2)(−3)) = 5/6. The area under x(t) is ∫₀<sup>∞</sup>e<sup>−2t</sup>dt + ∫<sub>−∞</sub><sup>0</sup>e<sup>3t</sup>dt = 1/2 + 1/3 = 5/6. The two agree, as they must, because X(0) = ∫x(t)dt.
examples.answer: X(s) = −5/((s + 2)(s − 3)), ROC −2 < Re(s) < 3; the Fourier transform exists because the strip contains the jω axis; X(0) = 5/6 = area under x(t).

examples.question: Find X(s) and the ROC of the pulse x(t) = u(t) − u(t − 2) (height 1, width 2 s).
steps: x(t) = 1 for 0 ≤ t < 2 and 0 elsewhere, so X(s) = ∫₀² e<sup>−st</sup>dt = (1 − e<sup>−2s</sup>)/s.
The signal has finite duration and finite area, so the ROC is the whole s-plane.
At s = 0 the formula reads 0/0. Expand e<sup>−2s</sup> ≈ 1 − 2s for small s: X(s) ≈ 2s/s = 2. So s = 0 is not a pole, and X(0) = 2 = the area of the pulse.
examples.answer: X(s) = (1 − e<sup>−2s</sup>)/s, ROC all s; there is no pole at s = 0 and X(0) = 2.

traps: Writing X(s) = 1/(s + 2) without Re(s) > −2. Without the ROC the answer could equally be −e<sup>−2t</sup>u(−t).
Putting the pole inside the ROC. The boundary of the ROC passes through a pole; the pole itself is never inside.
Using the one-sided integral for a signal such as e<sup>3t</sup>u(−t). The one-sided integral ignores t < 0 and gives 0 for that term; use the bilateral form.
Saying 'the ROC is to the right of the outermost pole'. For a right-sided signal it is to the right of the pole with the largest real part, whatever the size of its imaginary part.
Setting s = jω when the ROC does not contain the jω axis: e<sup>2t</sup>u(t) has X(s) = 1/(s − 2) with ROC Re(s) > 2, and no Fourier transform.

quiz.q: Write the bilateral Laplace transform and state what σ and ω are.
quiz.a: X(s) = ∫<sub>−∞</sub><sup>∞</sup>x(t)e<sup>−st</sup>dt with s = σ + jω; σ = Re(s) is the damping (s⁻¹) and ω = Im(s) is the angular frequency (rad/s).

quiz.q: What is the ROC of a finite-duration, absolutely integrable signal?
Why does the ROC always have vertical edges in the s-plane?
quiz.a: Convergence depends on |x(t)e<sup>−st</sup>| = |x(t)|e<sup>−σt</sup>, which involves σ only. If the integral converges at one s, it converges at every s with the same σ, so the ROC is bounded by lines σ = constant.

quiz.q: e<sup>2t</sup>u(t) has no Fourier transform but has a Laplace transform. Explain.
quiz.a: With σ > 2, e<sup>2t</sup>e<sup>−σt</sup> decays, so the integral converges: X(s) = 1/(s − 2), ROC Re(s) > 2. The Fourier transform needs σ = 0, which lies outside this ROC.

quiz.q: Find X(s) and the ROC of x(t) = e<sup>−5t</sup>u(t) + e<sup>−t</sup>u(t).
quiz.a: 1/(s + 5) + 1/(s + 1) = (2s + 6)/((s + 1)(s + 5)). Both terms are right-sided; the ROC is the overlap Re(s) > −1 (right of the rightmost pole, −1).

quiz.q: Find X(s) and the ROC of x(t) = e<sup>4t</sup>u(−t).
Does x(t) = e<sup>−3t</sup>u(−t) + e<sup>−t</sup>u(t) have a Laplace transform? Explain with the ROC.
quiz.a: The left-sided term e<sup>−3t</sup>u(−t) needs Re(s) < −3; the right-sided term e<sup>−t</sup>u(t) needs Re(s) > −1. No s satisfies both, so the ROC is empty and the transform does not exist.

quiz.q: X(s) = 1/((s + 1)(s − 2)). List every possible ROC and say what kind of signal each gives.
quiz.a: Re(s) > 2: right-sided; −1 < Re(s) < 2: two-sided (the only one containing the jω axis, so the only one with a Fourier transform); Re(s) < −1: left-sided.

beyond: Not for the exam. The inverse transform can also be written as the Bromwich integral, a line integral in the s-plane along a vertical line inside the ROC; complex-variable courses evaluate it with residues, which is where partial fractions come from. The Z-transform of discrete-time signals has the same ROC ideas with circles in place of vertical lines. Circuit simulators and control toolboxes work with transfer functions in s; search for 'pole-zero map' and 'Bromwich integral' to go further.

figure.caption: Three signals and their ROCs in the s-plane (× is a pole, the shaded part is the ROC). The first two share X(s) = 1/(s + 2) but lie on opposite sides of the pole at −2; the two-sided signal of the worked example has the strip between −2 and 3, which contains the jω axis, so its Fourier transform exists.
